slides.title: String algorithms
slides.main: All fast methods boil down to one idea: don't re-read what has already been read.

captions: The most common task: find a pattern in text
Second: tell how similar two strings are
Third: quickly tell which words start with a prefix

slides.title: Naive search
slides.main: Worst case is n · m: after a shift we forget everything we just learned.

captions: Pattern at the start: three letters match, the fourth fails
Shift by one, and the comparison starts over
Again almost the whole pattern, and again a miss at the end
Only at the fifth position we find it: about n · m comparisons

slides.title: Prefix function
slides.sub: A prefix that equals a suffix
slides.main: π[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix equal to a suffix of the substring up to i.

captions: For each position, find the longest prefix equal to its suffix
«aba»: starts with «a» and ends with «a», so the value is 1
«ababa»: «ab» at the start and «ab» at the end, so the value is 2
Whole string: «aba» at both the start and the end, so the value is 3

slides.title: Computed in one pass
slides.sub: k grows by one and drops in jumps
slides.main: Jumps down never outnumber steps right, so the time is linear.

captions: Previous value k = 2: try to extend the match with the letter d
d is not c, but we don't need to start over
Take k = π[k − 1] = π[1] = 0 and try again
d is not a: π[5] = 0; k only dropped, and it grew by one at a time

slides.title: Knuth–Morris–Pratt search
slides.main: The text pointer never goes back: time on the order of n + m.

captions: Three letters matched, the fourth missed: we already know something
k = π[2] = 1: the pattern shifts by i − k = 2, no re-reading of the text
Another miss, k = π[0] = 0: shift the pattern by one more
Pointer i never went back: match at position 3

slides.title: Periods and compression
slides.main: Period = length − π[last]; if the length divides evenly, the string is a repetition of the period.

captions: A string made by repeating one piece
The last prefix function value is six: a border of length 6
Period = length − border = 9 − 6 = 3

slides.title: Z-function
slides.main: The Z-block moves only to the right, so everything is computed in linear time.

captions: z[i] is how many characters from position i match the beginning of the string
For aabxaab this is —, 1, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0
Inside the Z-block we peek the value from the mirror position

slides.title: What to choose
slides.main: «Border» and «period»: prefix function; «common beginning from a position»: Z-function.

captions: Both carry the same information in different forms
Prefix function: what is both at the start and at the end
Z-function: how much matches the beginning at each position
One converts into the other in linear time

frames.text: convert to each other in O(n)

slides.title: String hashing
slides.main: A substring hash comes from two prefix hashes; equal hashes don't yet mean equal strings.

captions: Each letter is a number; for clarity take the base equal to 10
H[i + 1] = H[i] · 10 + s[i]: every prefix gets a number
Hash of «bc» = H[3] − H[1] · 100 = 123 − 100 = 23: constant time
Equal hashes don't prove equal strings: check the strings after that

slides.title: Rabin–Karp algorithm
slides.main: The window shifts in constant time; a matching hash is a reason to check the characters.

captions: Pattern hash is 415; compute the hash of a window of the same length
Window shifted: remove the departed digit, add the new one, in constant time
Window hash equals pattern hash: a candidate is found
Compare the characters directly to guard against collisions

slides.title: Trie
slides.main: Insertion and lookup take the word length; words with a prefix come from a subtree traversal.

captions: Edges are letters; the path to a marked node is a word. A shared start is stored once
Looking up the word ten: three steps along the letters, regardless of dictionary size
Prefix te: descend along it and traverse the subtree: tea, ten
Insertion and lookup take as many steps as the word has letters

slides.title: Levenshtein distance
slides.main: Dynamic programming over an n × m table; two rows are enough to store.

captions: Zero row and column: turning into the empty string and back
Cell (i, j) is the distance between the prefixes of lengths i and j
Letters differ: take the minimum of three neighbors and add 1
The bottom right corner is the answer: one replacement turns cat into cut

frames.text: rows are filled left to right

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Ask yourself: what information am I throwing away that could be remembered?

captions: The prefix and Z-function tables store how a string matches itself
A hash is a comparison of numbers; a trie is a dictionary with prefixes
Levenshtein tells how close strings are
